column4: The section joins what falls away with what is held and written. This verse says that not even a leaf falls without God's knowledge, and that what is moist or dry is in a clear book; the falling object and the preserved record meet in one ayah.

The section moves from what is left behind to what is preserved in a record. This verse says God knows what the earth diminishes from the dead and that with Him is a preserving book, joining disappearance with a record that keeps account.

The section names Moses' pages and defines a reminder as what recalls a needed matter. This verse says God wrote admonition and detailed instruction for Moses on the tablets, giving a concrete written source of reminder.
This continues Moses' tablets after he takes them up again: their inscription contains guidance and mercy for those who fear their Lord. It adds the content and audience of the written reminder.

This repeats the prophetic pattern of reciting God's signs, purifying the audience, and teaching the Book. Its own address says the Messenger also teaches what the people did not know, extending the section's meeting of recitation, purification, and scripture to its immediate audience.

The section joins recitation, remembrance, and prayer through the surah's named roots. This verse commands reciting the Book and establishing prayer, then says remembrance of God is greater, bringing those acts together and adding prayer's effect in its context.

The section says Allah gathers and has the Prophet recite revelation, while a dictionary branch names speech transmitted from another. Here opponents allege that the Quran is old tales written down and dictated to the Prophet; the ayah supplies a specific human-copying counterclaim to the section's account of divinely given recitation.

The section links recitation with written pages and earlier scripture. This verse says the Prophet had not recited a book before the Quran or written one with his hand; its own contribution is to distinguish his prior state from the revelation whose pages the section describes.

The section describes prophetic books as reminders that are held in written pages. This verse says the rabbis and scholars were entrusted with God's Book and charged to preserve it, making custodianship of revealed scripture explicit.

The section says the Quran's message is also present in earlier prophetic books. This verse describes the Quran as confirming the earlier Scripture and overseeing it, specifying the relation between the present recitation and prior revelation.

The section names Moses among the holders of the earlier pages. This verse says God gave Moses guidance and caused the Israelites to inherit the Book, directly extending the transmission of Moses' scripture to a later community.

This completes 40:53 by calling that inherited Book guidance and a reminder for people of understanding. It directly joins Moses' scripture to the section's dictionary sense of prophetic books as remembrance.

After the debt-writing instructions in 2:282, this verse says that when people trust one another without a written pledge, the entrusted party must discharge the trust. Its own contribution is a concrete safeguard against losing what was entrusted.

The section's dictionary defines forgetting as failing to keep what was entrusted. This verse commands that trusts be returned to their rightful owners, stating the affirmative counterpart to letting an entrusted thing go.

The section explicitly sets forgetting against حفظ, keeping or guarding what was entrusted. Joseph offers himself as “حَفِيظٌ عَلِيمٌ” over the storehouses, giving a concrete instance of guarding an entrusted provision, though here the object is grain rather than remembered revelation.
